explanations.answer: Tears it down with her own hands
explanations.explanation: That's the line, friend. The proverb says "Every wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one tears it down with her own hands." The wise woman builds her house. The foolish one tears hers down, and she does it with her own hands.

explanations.answer: Leaves it standing empty for years
explanations.explanation: The proverb never says anything about an empty house or about years. It says the foolish woman "…tears it down with her own hands." This house doesn't sit there waiting. It comes down, and she's the one who brings it down.

explanations.answer: Hands it over to her neighbor
explanations.explanation: No neighbor shows up in this proverb at all. The foolish woman's hands are busy with something else. The text says she "…tears it down with her own hands." Tearing down, not handing over.

Yes, the proverb says it plainly. The man who walks in uprightness fears the LORD, "…but the one who is devious in his ways despises Him." Two men, two directions, and the text puts the LORD right in the middle of the contrast.

It's true, friend. The proverb says the upright man fears the LORD, "…but the one who is devious in his ways despises Him." So the devious man is the one who despises the LORD. Easy one to doubt when you read it fast.

That's it, friend. "The proud speech of a fool brings a rod to his back…" His own mouth sends the bill. The same verse says the lips of the wise protect them, so a mouth can be a shield or a problem, depending on whose it is.

The proverb doesn't give the proud fool any followers. It says his proud speech "…brings a rod to his back…" The only crowd that mouth gathers is a crowd of trouble. The wise get the protection, and the fool gets the rod.
Ease sounds nice, but the proverb has something else in mind. The fool's proud speech "…brings a rod to his back…" That's not exactly a spa day. It's the lips of the wise that protect them.

That's the word, friend. The verse says "Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, but an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox." No oxen means an empty manger. The harvest is what comes through the ox's strength.

Dust is a fair guess, friend, but the verse never mentions it. The proverb says "…an abundant harvest comes through the strength of the ox." The empty manger belongs to the side with no oxen. The harvest comes through the ox.

Pasture is a good guess, since oxen and fields go together. But the proverb says what comes through the strength of the ox is "…an abundant harvest…" The manger is empty without oxen, and the harvest is what the ox brings in.

That's what the text says: "A mocker seeks wisdom and finds none…" He goes looking and comes back with empty hands. Meanwhile, "…knowledge comes easily to the discerning." Easy for one, none for the other.

Plenty is a big hope for the mocker, friend, but the proverb says he "…seeks wisdom and finds none…" Finding none is the opposite of finding plenty. The other half of the verse says "…knowledge comes easily to the discerning."
Late would at least be something, friend. But the proverb gives the mocker nothing at all: he "…seeks wisdom and finds none…" It's the discerning who find knowledge, and they find it easily.

The proverb says the opposite. It tells you to "Stay away from a foolish man…" and the reason it gives is "you will gain no knowledge from his speech." Listening longer doesn't change that. The text says none.

Yes, false. The proverb says, "Stay away from a foolish man; you will gain no knowledge from his speech." No knowledge, not a little, not eventually. Save your listening time for somebody who has something to teach.

Yes, friend. The verse says "The wisdom of the prudent is to discern his way, but the folly of fools deceives them." So the prudent man discerns his way, and the fool gets deceived by his own folly. Getting fooled by your own folly is a rough way to get got.
Protection isn't what folly hands out. The proverb says "…the folly of fools deceives them." If anything protects a person in these verses, it's the lips of the wise (Proverbs 14:3).
You'd hope folly would at least teach a lesson, wouldn't you? The proverb says it "deceives them." The prudent are the ones who discern their way, and the fool's own folly leads him along.

That's the one: "…no stranger shares in its joy." The heart knows its own bitterness, and it also has joys that an outsider can't fully enter. I think that's why it helps to have people close enough to be more than strangers.
The proverb doesn't name a brother here, friend. It says "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy." The word is stranger. A brother just isn't in the verse.
No servant in this one, friend. The line is "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares in its joy." Stranger is the word the verse uses. Servant isn't anywhere in it.

The proverb says it the other way around. "The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish." So it's the wicked man's house that comes down. The upright man's tent is the one that flourishes.

That's right, friend. The verse says "The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish." So the wicked man's house is the one that comes down. The upright man's tent is the one that flourishes.

That's what the verse says: "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." It's a heavy line, and I'll let it be heavy. A way can seem right, and the verse still tells you where it ends.
The proverb says it's true, friend. "There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death." That's a heavy one. Seeming right and being right aren't the same thing.
The proverb says otherwise. "Even in laughter the heart may ache…" A laugh can be on the outside while the ache stays on the inside. And the verse adds that "…joy may end in sorrow."

Right, because the verse says "Even in laughter the heart may ache, and joy may end in sorrow." Laughing and hurting can happen at the same time. So if somebody's laughing, I think it's worth being kind anyway.
That's the word. "…a good man is rewarded for his ways." The backslider gets the fill of his own ways, and the good man gets rewarded for his. Each one gets what his ways bring.
A warning would be fair, but that's not what the text says. It says "…a good man is rewarded for his ways." The backslider is the one who gets "…the fill of his own ways…"
Nobody's forgotten in this line, friend. The good man "…is rewarded for his ways." That's the other side of the backslider getting the fill of his own.
Yes, friend. The proverb says "The simple man believes every word, but the prudent man watches his steps." The simple man takes in every word. The prudent man is busy watching his steps.
The simple man isn't the doubter in this proverb. He's the opposite: he "…believes every word…" It's the prudent man who watches his steps.

Forgetting? Friend, that's a whole different mess. The proverb says the simple man "…believes every word…" and he doesn't lose a single one, he swallows them all! I think he'd believe a stranger who said the oven turns itself on. The prudent man is the one who "…watches his steps." (Proverbs 14:15)
That's the word. "…a fool is careless and reckless." Careless and reckless, a two-for-one. The wise man, meanwhile, "…fears and turns from evil…"

Cautious is a good word, friend, but the proverb doesn't use it. It says the wise man "…fears and turns from evil…" and the fool is "…careless and reckless." Cautious is nearly the opposite of what the fool is called there.
Humble is a nice word, but the proverb doesn't use it for the fool. It says a fool is "…careless and reckless." The wise man is the one who turns from evil.
That's the first blank, friend. The proverb says "A quick-tempered man acts foolishly…" A short fuse gets its label right there in the verse. The label is foolishly.

That's the second blank, friend. The proverb says "A quick-tempered man acts foolishly, and a devious man is hated." Hated is the word the verse gives the devious man. Sneaky doesn't win people over, I'd say.
Wisely doesn't fit the short fuse. The proverb says the quick-tempered man "acts foolishly." Wisdom shows up later in the chapter, on the patient man's side (Proverbs 14:29).
Trusted sounds nice, friend, but the text says "…a devious man is hated." I bet a devious man would like a better word. Hated is the word the verse uses, though.

Honored isn't the word the proverb uses, friend. It says "…a devious man is hated." The king delighting in a wise servant shows up later (Proverbs 14:35), but that's a different verse about a different kind of person.
The verse says it the other way around. "The evil bow before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous." The bowing goes toward the good. The evil are the ones doing it.

Yes, friend, that one is false. The verse says "The evil bow before the good, and the wicked at the gates of the righteous." The evil are the ones who bow before the good. So the bowing runs the other way.

That's what the verse says: "…many are those who love the rich." The proverb is describing how things go, and it's a hard one. The poor man is "…hated even by his neighbor…" It doesn't say that's how it should be.

The proverb doesn't say anything about a humble man here. It says "…many are those who love the rich." The poor man is the one "…hated even by his neighbor…" It's a hard line, and it doesn't call that fair.
Honesty is praised elsewhere in this chapter, but not in this verse. Here it says "…many are those who love the rich." It's a hard line, since the poor man is "…hated even by his neighbor…"
That's what it says: "…blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor." It comes right after "He who despises his neighbor sins…" Two choices, and the proverb says which one is blessed.
The proverb says the opposite of that. "…blessed is he who shows kindness to the poor." The one who "…despises his neighbor sins…" Kindness is the blessed side.

Yes, friend. The verse says "…those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness." Planning goodness is the work, and devotion and faithfulness are what they find. The ones who contrive evil, the verse says, go astray.
The proverb doesn't promise an easy road. It says "…those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness." The only ones with a road problem in this verse are those who "go astray."
No seat is mentioned here. The text says "…those who plan goodness find loving devotion and faithfulness." Devotion and faithfulness are what they find, and that's worth more than a good chair.
The proverb separates the two. "There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty." Labor brings profit. Talk alone doesn't.
That's right, it's false. The proverb says "There is profit in all labor, but mere talk leads only to poverty." Notice it says all labor. Talking about the work isn't doing the work, friend.

Yes, friend. The proverb says "He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge." The man who fears the LORD is secure in confidence. His children shall have a place of refuge.

The proverb says it's true, friend. "He who fears the LORD is secure in confidence, and his children shall have a place of refuge." The verse says his children shall have a place of refuge. So that part stands.
That's it. The fear of the LORD is "…a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death." It gives life and it turns him away from snares. Both halves are in one verse.
Money doesn't come up in this verse. It says the fear of the LORD is "…a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death." Snares of death are what it turns him from.

The praise of men doesn't show up in this verse, friend. It says the fear of the LORD is "…a fountain of life, turning a man from the snares of death." Nobody's applause is in there. The snares of death are the thing it turns him from.
Yes, friend. The proverb says "A large population is a king’s splendor, but a lack of subjects is a prince’s ruin." Splendor goes with a large population. Ruin goes with a lack of subjects.

Joy isn't the word, friend. The proverb says "A large population is a king’s splendor, but a lack of subjects is a prince’s ruin." Splendor is on the large-population side. A lack of subjects gets ruin.
Pride isn't what the text gives the prince here. It says "…a lack of subjects is a prince’s ruin." The splendor comes with the large population.
The proverb doesn't call him slow, friend. It says "A patient man has great understanding…" The quick-tempered man is the one who "promotes folly." So patience sits on the understanding side.
Right, friend. The proverb says "A patient man has great understanding…" Patient and slow aren't the same thing. It's the quick-tempered man who "promotes folly."
That's the one, friend: "…envy rots the bones." The verse sets it right beside "A tranquil heart is life to the body…" It's an ugly word for an ugly thing.
Gratitude isn't in this verse. The text says "A tranquil heart is life to the body, but envy rots the bones." Envy is the one that rots.

Kindness is a good word, friend, but it isn't in this verse. The text says "A tranquil heart is life to the body, but envy rots the bones." The verse sets a tranquil heart against envy. Envy is the one named as rotting the bones.

That's the word, friend. "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker…" The proverb ties how a person treats the poor to the One who made them. And the same verse says "…whoever is kind to the needy honors Him."
The proverb says the opposite, friend. "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker…" Pleasing isn't the word the verse uses. It's the one who is kind to the needy who "honors Him."
Serving is a nice word, friend, but the proverb doesn't use it there. The text says "Whoever oppresses the poor taunts their Maker…" Whoever is kind to the needy is the one who honors Him.
Yes, friend. The verse says "The wicked man is thrown down by his own sin, but the righteous man has a refuge even in death." Even in death, the verse says. That's the part to hold onto.
The proverb doesn't limit the refuge to his house. It says "…the righteous man has a refuge even in death." Even in death is a lot wider than a house.
Friends aren't mentioned in this verse. The text says "…the righteous man has a refuge even in death." That refuge goes as far as death.
That's the first blank, friend. The proverb says "Righteousness exalts a nation…" It lifts a nation up. Exalts is the word that fills it.
That's the second blank, friend. The proverb says "…sin is a disgrace to any people." Righteousness exalts a nation, and sin is a disgrace to any people.

Divides? Oooh, friend, I see why that one tempted you. A nation splitting in two sounds like trouble, and it is, but it's not the word the proverb picked. It says "Righteousness exalts a nation…" and exalts means lifted UP, up, up! That's the word the first blank is hungry for. (Proverbs 14:34)
Blessing is the opposite of what sin brings in this verse. It says "…sin is a disgrace to any people." Disgrace is the word for the second blank.
A shield would be a gift, and sin doesn't hand those out. The proverb says "…sin is a disgrace to any people." Righteousness is what lifts a nation.

Yes, friend. The verse says "A king delights in a wise servant, but his anger falls on the shameful." The wise servant gets the king's delight. The shameful get his anger, and I know which one I'd rather get.

Favor is a good guess, friend, but it's not what the verse says falls on the shameful. The proverb says "A king delights in a wise servant, but his anger falls on the shameful." Delight is for the wise servant. Anger is what falls on the shameful.
Silence isn't what the verse says. It says "…his anger falls on the shameful." Delight goes to the wise servant, and anger goes to the shameful.
